You are an experienced Decent DE1 barista choosing an espresso profile and starting recipe for a specific coffee.

You get: the coffee as the roaster and the bag describe it, a rules-based ranking of community profiles with each profile's own description (from its author), a suggested recipe per profile, the user's setup and preferences, and their past shots of this bag.

How to choose:
- Read the roaster's description (roast level, what it's roasted for, process, tasting notes, blend or single origin, any published recipe) and match it to what each profile is designed to bring out. Trust the profile authors' own guidance over generic rules.
- The rules ranking is a strong prior, not a verdict. Pick a lower-ranked candidate when the coffee's description clearly fits it better, and say why.
- Past shots outrank everything: repeat what scored well, and move away from what didn't.
- profileTitle MUST be one of the candidate titles, copied exactly.
- Keep dose, yield and temperature close to that candidate's suggested recipe unless you have a reason (a roaster recipe, past shots, the milk preference).
- dialIn: specific guidance for this coffee on this profile (targets like dripping weight, flow rate or shot time, and which way to grind first).
- rationale: 2–4 short bullets in plain words that connect the coffee's description to the profile. alternatives: up to 2 other candidates worth trying next, each with a one-line reason.
- grindHint is relative guidance; you don't know the user's grinder numbers unless past shots include them.

output.grindHint: Start about 1 step finer than your medium-roast setting. This is a light roast, but anaerobic naturals extract easily, so you don't need to go as fine as you would for a dense washed light roast.
output.restAdvice: There's no roast date on file. Light-roast anaerobic naturals usually taste best about 14–40 days off roast. If the bag is under 2 weeks old, expect gassy, uneven shots and harsher ferment notes. Add the roast date so rest can be tracked.
output.dialIn: Pull 18 g to 40 g and aim for 25–35 s. Keep the profile's falling temperature and change only the starting temperature. If the shot is sour or thin, grind finer first. If the rum note turns hot and boozy or the finish is drying, grind coarser or drop the start to 84 °C. If it's sweet but muted, raise it to 86–87 °C.
rationale: A 72-hour anaerobic natural extracts easily and has a lot of ferment character. A lower, falling temperature keeps the strawberry-jam sweetness clean, so the rum note doesn't turn harsh.
This profile is built for clarity, sweetness and fruit, which suits a jammy single-origin Pink Bourbon you're drinking straight.
A normal 1:2.2 ratio keeps enough body for the cacao-nib finish. A very long shot could wash that out.
It's ranked second for light roasts and is more forgiving than the high-extraction profiles on an unfamiliar bag with no past shots.

alternatives.why: Try this if you want the biggest fruit (18 g to 90 g at about 91.5 °C). Expect more clarity and acidity but less jammy body.
Try this for more layered fruit and aroma. Aim for about 8 g dripping before the ramp, and lower the temperature a little if the ferment notes take over.

rationale: The roaster roasted this medium-dark Brazil natural for espresso, which is exactly the kind of coffee Londonium was written for.
The lever-style pressure decline brings out heavy body and the chocolate and dried-fruit notes on the bag, and keeps roast bitterness down.
A thick, syrupy shot cuts through milk well, which suits your milk drinks.
It's forgiving of imperfect puck prep, and that helps when you're dialing in a new bag. I cut the yield slightly from the profile's 42 g to 40 g so the shot stands up better in milk.

alternatives.why: Same lever style, a little hotter and with a tighter 1:2 ratio. Try it if you want more punch and dried-fruit sweetness in milk.
Lower pressure and lower acidity, and it suits naturals. Use it if Londonium shots come out bitter or channel.

output.restAdvice: There's no roast date, so check the bag. Dark roasts are usually best 4–21 days after roasting. If the beans are very fresh and foam a lot during preinfusion, give them a few more days.
output.dialIn: You have no scale, so let the DE1's volumetric stop end the shot at about 40 g. Judge the grind by time: first drops should show near the end of preinfusion (roughly 8–15 s), and the whole shot should take 30–45 s, with peak pressure around 8–9 bar. If it runs faster than 30 s or tastes thin in milk, grind one step finer. If it runs past 45 s or tastes bitter or ashy, grind coarser first, then try lowering the temperature to 86 °C.
rationale: The profile is written for dark roasts, and the author says it's 'like having a milkshake with extra syrup'. That big body suits a heavy Brazil and Monsooned Malabar blend.
It brings out the body and chocolate the roaster lists (dark chocolate, molasses), and those cut through milk well.
Its extra preinfusion steps make up for imperfect puck prep, which helps while you're learning.
The low 87.5 °C keeps a dark roast from turning bitter or ashy. The yield is slightly shorter than the profile's 42 g, which keeps the shot thick for milk.

alternatives.why: Try this if your shots keep channelling or tasting harsh. It only peaks at 6 bar, and its author suggests it for when you're having trouble making good drinks.
Decent's own go-to for milk drinks. It's very tolerant and makes a simple chocolatey backup if the lever-style shot feels hard to control.

The low starting temperature (87 °C) and the forgiving extra steps help keep dark-roast bitterness down.
Trimming yield from 42 g to 40 g makes the shot a bit stronger so it stands up in milk.

output.grindHint: Start at your usual medium-roast setting, or one step coarser as the baseline suggests. Decaf beans are brittle and make more fines, so they can run fast or choke without warning. Let the first shot tell you which way to go before making big changes.
output.restAdvice: The bag has no roast date. Medium-roast decaf usually tastes best about 7–28 days after roasting. If you know the roast date, add it so rest can be tracked.
output.dialIn: Aim for the first drips around 8–12 s into infusion, then a steady main pour of about 1.8–2.0 ml/s at no more than 9 bar, ending at 38 g in 28–38 s. If it gushes before 25 s or tastes thin in milk, grind finer. If it tastes sharp, bitter or dry, grind coarser or lower the temperature to 86 °C before you change anything else.
rationale: Medium roast roasted for espresso: D-Flow's default settings were written for exactly this roast level.
D-Flow moves to the next step based on dripped weight, so it adjusts to decaf's unpredictable flow, which is useful when you have no past shots to go on yet.
It brings out body and sweetness, which suits the milk chocolate and panela notes and helps the shot hold up in milk.
87.5 °C is fairly cool, which suits decaf: it extracts easily, and running hotter tends to bring out woody, bitter tastes.

alternatives.why: A lever-style shot with a big, syrupy body that makes chocolate notes stronger in a flat white or latte, if D-Flow tastes a little light in milk.
Its lower 6 bar peak is very forgiving of channelling. Fall back to it if this decaf keeps channelling or tasting harsh.

output.grindHint: Start coarse for espresso, about where you'd grind a medium roast or a touch coarser. This profile needs a coarse grind even for a very light filter roast, and small grind changes move the pressure a lot.
output.restAdvice: There's no roast date on the bag. Light filter roasts from Ethiopia usually taste best about 14–40 days after roasting. If it's fresher than 2 weeks, expect channeling and a sharp edge, and give it more time.
output.dialIn: Aim for a peak of 8–9 bar and 90 g out in 35–40 s. If the peak is under 8 bar or the shot runs fast, go up 0.5 g in dose before you change the grind. Only adjust the grind once the dose is close, and in very small steps. If the cup tastes thin or sour at the right time, raise the temperature to 94–95°C. If it tastes drying or bitter, drop the dose by 0.5 g or grind slightly coarser.
rationale: This is a washed Guji roasted for filter, so it's very light. The allongé's long 1:5 ratio and high extraction suit coffees like this.
Peach, jasmine and black tea are delicate, clear notes. The allongé brings out fruit and florals with tea-like clarity rather than a heavy body.
You're drinking it straight, and flat burrs give even, high-extraction grounds. That suits a coarse, high-flow profile with no milk.
I set the temperature 1°C above the profile's 92°C because filter-roast beans can be hard to extract.

alternatives.why: Try this if you want a more concentrated shot (18 g in, about 50 g out, 95°C) that keeps the clarity but has more syrupy peach. Aim for about 8 g dripping before the pressure ramp.
Try this if the Rao Allongé tastes good but a little underdeveloped. It extracts even more (about 26%) at the same 1:5 ratio, with a finer grind and a shot of about 60 s.
